newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico unveils 1997 budget, calls for growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico unveils 1997 budget, calls for growth.

text.p: Mexico unveiled a 1997 budget on Thursday that calls for greater government spending for the first time since the 1994 peso crash threw the economy into crisis and forced the government to tighten its belt.

Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz outlined a budget that calls for a deficit of 0.5 percent of gross domestic product -- an effort to boost the country's sluggish economic recovery and help real wages rise for the first time in three years.
The government forecast economic growth of 4.0 percent next year, and said the economy would finish this year with growth of about 3.7 percent -- higher than its original 3.0 percent forecast.

Ortiz said Mexico would keep the free-floating peso, and it said it used an average exchange rate of 8.53 pesos per dollar next year as part of its budget assumptions. The peso is currently trading at about 7.93 per dollar.
The budget also targets 1997 inflation at 15 percent, following 26.2 percent inflation this year -- above the 20.2 percent originally forecast by the government.

The budget calls for revenues of 694.9 billion pesos, a real increase of 3.8 percent, and spending of 710.79 billion pesos, up 5.8 percent in real terms. The planned budget shortfall is 15.89 billion pesos.
Revenues will benefit from a 10.3 percent real increase in tax receipts. It is the first time in three years that the government has forecast higher tax receipts.

Although there will be no new taxes in the budget, the government said higher tax receipts would come from more aggressive collection efforts. Currently, only about a fourth of Mexican workers pay taxes.
A 10.3 percent rise in receipts from Petroleos Mexicanos, Mexico's state-owned oil company, will also boost revenue.

Government spending will try to target the poor ahead of next year's midterm election. Social spending is slated to grow 9.3 percent in real terms -- totaling 55.8 percent of the total programmed budget.

Total public investment is slated to grow 25 percent, the highest rate in 10 years, according to the government. Public investment will equal 3.7 percent of GDP, focused mostly on infrastructure projects in the oil sector, electricity, highways, water and housing.

The government budget takes into account the huge tab for an ongoing bank bailout program and a new private pension system, which will reduce the amount of money sent into government coffers by state workers from July next year.
The tab for both is expected to be 1.02 percent of GDP next year, according to the budget.
"Public finances next year will need to absorb the costs of these programs," Ortiz told legislators.
Ortiz estimated that Mexico's 1997 current account deficit would be about 1.2 percent of GDP.
He said economic growth next year will be based on export growth, stepped-up public and private investment, and a gradual recovery of consumption, according to the text of the budget.
Ortiz said the investment in the export sector and projected economic growth by Mexico's main trading partners should allow Mexican exports to fuel a recovery.
He also said a "gradual recovery" in real wages next year would allow for "a moderate" recovery of consumption.
